# Python code-quality CLI: wrong scores, dropped paths and swallowed errors, diagnosed without a test suite

A command-line tool that reads Python sources and reports numbers about them now gets a great many of those numbers, and several of the things it writes out, wrong. Nothing about the Python being measured changed and nobody touched the way the tool is invoked; the same commands that used to print sensible figures now print figures that are too low, leave whole sections empty, disregard what was written down in settings files, or stop with an error where they used to succeed. The repository has received 29 separate undocumented edits.

Telling it what to look at goes wrong first. Handing it the same source file under several spellings at once — a relative one, the same one written with a redundant up-and-back step, and the full absolute one — no longer folds them into a single entry printed under the first spelling given; the run fails outright, and asking the tool afterwards to translate the absolute spelling back into the one it printed fails as well. Invoking a check with a single directory or file argument now behaves as though that argument had never been given: settings are looked up relative to the wrong place, so a strict settings file sitting in an outer directory now gates a nested checkout that carries its own repository marker, and the repeated-code check no longer fails on a package holding a file that cannot be parsed.
